segments.line: Here's the problem nobody thinks about.
Water doesn't climb up to your tap by itself. Electric pumps push it there. When the pumps stop, the pipes lose pressure, and
the taps go dry. In
2003, a blackout cut the water pressure around Detroit.
A hundred and twenty- six communities were told to boil their water. That's real. And that blackout
lasted two days. Yours lasts forever. And
the toilets? They need water pressure too. By day four, your whole building smells like it. Then
the food. A
fridge keeps food safe for about four hours without power. A full freezer, about two days. That's real too.
After that, everything you didn't eat at the barbecue starts to rot. And
the shops can't refill. Trucks need fuel, and the pump at every gas station is electric.
The shelves empty in a day. Nothing comes back. Your
mom fills every pot, every bottle and the bathtub with the last water from the tap.
Smart. Because that bathtub is now the most important thing your family owns. And when it gets
dark, it gets really dark. The candles burn down. By day four, your family goes
to bed at sunset, like people did for most of human history. Then there's
the biggest problem of all. In
nineteen hundred, before most homes had electricity, about one point six billion people lived on Earth. Today, more than eight billion do. How do you feed eight billion people?
Machines, cold trucks, water pumps, and fertilizer made in giant factories.
Scientists estimate that factory- made fertilizer feeds about half the people alive today. That's real.
Without power, the factories stop. The tractors with computers stop. The pumps that water the fields stop.
So the real danger isn't the dark. It's
dinner.
